newsitem.title: MALI: Four declare candidacy for Mali presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Four declare candidacy for Mali presidential poll.

text.p: Oumar Konare and three challengers have declared their candidacy for Mali's presidential elections next month, political party officials said on Thursday. Konare was nominated by his
ruling Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADAMA), which launched the historian to power in Mali's widely praised 1992 democratic transition.
He will be seeking a second five-year term in the election scheduled for May 4 with a runoff on May 18.

The other contenders are Zoumana Sacko of the People's Convention Party who was prime minister in the 1991 transition government; Seydou Badian Kouyate of the socialist US-RDA who was a minister in Mali's 1960-68 independence cabinet and teacher Mohamed Lamine Trore, national secretary of the Movement for African Independence, Renaissance and Integration party.
Nine candidates contested Mali's first multi-party presidential poll in 1992.
Parliamentary elections are set for April 13, more than a month later than planned. The second round is on April 27.
The Independent National Electoral Commission CENI had requested that legislative elections be put back from March 9 and March 23, citing organisational delays.
Municipal elections are scheduled for June 1 to wrap up Mali's second multi-party polls since the transition.
Konare's ADAMA had a majority in the old 116-seat national assembly. The new assembly will have 147 seats.
The opposition is grouped in two main opposition alliances, the Rally of Patriotic Forces (RFP) and Front for Change and Democracy (FCD).
Thirteen opposition deputies placed a no confidence motion before parliament, accusing the government of being unable to organise elections within the constitutional deadline.
Parliament rejected the motion on Tuesday.
Parliament's mandate ends on April 17, Konare's on June 8.
Mali's last elections followed the 1991 overthrow of dictator Moussa Traore by soldiers, led by General Amadou Toumani Toure, who ushered in civilian rule and stepped down.
